content.question_text: What problem does the pattern matching form of instanceof solve compared to the traditional instanceof check?

core_requirements: The traditional form requires mentioning the subclass type three times: in the instanceof check, in the cast, and in the variable declaration.
The pattern matching form lets you declare the subclass variable directly in the instanceof test, eliminating the need for a separate cast.
acceptable_variations: Pattern matching combines the instanceof check and cast into one step.

content.question_text: What happens to the pattern variable if the instanceof check fails?

core_requirements: If the object doesn't match the type, the pattern variable is not set.
The instanceof operator yields false and the body of the if statement is skipped.
acceptable_variations: The variable is unbound and the condition is false — the if block does not execute.

content.question_text: Why is it a compile-time error to write 'if (boss instanceof Employee e)' when boss is already declared as type Manager?

core_requirements: It is a useless instanceof pattern — since boss is already known to be a Manager, which is a subclass of Employee, it is always an Employee.
The compiler detects this as pointless and flags it as a compile-time error.
acceptable_variations: The pattern is always true so it's useless — the compiler rejects it.

content.question_text: Why can a pattern variable introduced by instanceof be used immediately on the right-hand side of a && expression, but not with ||?

core_requirements: With &&, the right-hand side is only evaluated if the left-hand side is true. If the instanceof matched, the variable is bound and safe to use.
With ||, the right-hand side is evaluated when the left-hand side is false — in that case the instanceof failed and the variable was never bound, making it a compile-time error.
acceptable_variations: && guarantees the left side is true before evaluating right side; || does not — so the variable may be unbound.
